connector: Hello, it’s Diana. Anne’s thirteen now, and she says it makes her feel ever so much older and wiser. Miss Stacy wants us to write a story out of our own heads for Monday, which is simply terrible. I can manage to write about the woods, but a whole story? Anne has a plan, though. Anne always has a plan.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Diana. Today is about our story club, and how Anne works out what she thinks a good story is. She has a great many ideas about it. Before the reading there’s word work, doing words that don’t follow the usual rule for the past, and a spelling rule about a quiet letter e. Then you’ll tell the chapter in a few sentences. Just a few. Anne would need fifty.
transcripts.wgrd: The box says to tell a chapter in three sentences, not thirty. I’m rather good at that, because I never know what to do with my people, so I simply stop. Anne is the opposite. She keeps every lovely word and every sigh. So as you read, stop now and then and ask what has changed. If nothing has, that part can go.
transcripts.dol: The top sentence is Anne’s, and it’s about Matthew, who likes every story she writes. Look at the two doing words that tell what already happened. Neither one takes the usual ending. The bottom sentence is about me, I’m afraid, and somebody forgot my capital. There’s also a story that belongs to someone, and a sentence that never stops. Mend all three.
transcripts.guide1: Four bits of word work, and two of them sort into three columns, not two. That’s harder than it sounds. Ruby would put everything in the middle and hope. Don’t do that. Say each word out loud before you move it, because your ear knows more than you think. And the fill-ins want the back half of each word, not the front. Read the meaning first.
transcripts.morphology: Two old roots today, living inside words you already use. One means to carry. The other means to pull, or to draw. The front of each word is already there, and you type the rest. Read the meaning after the blank first. Then ask yourself, is something being carried here, or pulled? Think of a wagon, and then think of a magnet. That settles most of them.
transcripts.vocabulary: Four new words, and each card has a real sentence from the book above it. Some of those sentences come from chapters you haven’t reached yet, so don’t worry if you don’t know who’s talking. Use the sentence anyway, then look for word parts, then guess before you flip. Anne flips first and thinks afterward. I’d think first. Then tap.
transcripts.grammar: All of these doing words are already in the past, and not one of them takes the usual ending. But they break the rule in three different ways. Say each pair out loud, the now word and then the past one. Listen for how much changes. A little, a lot, or nothing at all. Anne says breaking a rule beautifully is half the fun. Here it’s the whole lesson.
transcripts.spelling: These words all end in a quiet e, and then something gets added. Sometimes the e stays and sometimes it goes. Look at the first letter of what’s been added, and look at what comes just before the e. Those two together decide it. One column is for words that never had the tricky sound at all. You’ll know them when you say them.
transcripts.copia: That sentence is about me, and it’s quite true. I did write to Aunt Josephine about our club. Now say it three ways. Change the doing word first, but keep it about a letter. Then start the sentence somewhere else, with a when or a where. Then tell how I wrote it. Anne says one sentence said three ways is three times as good. I only half believe her.
transcripts.guide2: There’s a box here about learning from your mistakes. I know a little about that. Anne and I made up the Haunted Wood together, and we frightened ourselves so badly that neither of us would go through it after dark. Anne says it cured her of letting her imagination run away with her. As you read, watch whether it has. I’m not sure it has.
transcripts.read: Two stops. The first comes when Anne tells how each girl in the club writes. One of them is me, and I’ll say no more. Think about why four friends would make up such different stories. The second comes at the very end. Ask yourself why none of us ever writes about Avonlea. It’s right outside the window, and nobody thinks of it at all.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write, and it’s your answers, not your stories. Miss Stacy says a good answer points to the place in the book. So when a question asks what happened, say it plainly, then show where. When it asks why, give a reason and a line to back it up. And keep your summary short. Short is hard. I know, because Anne never manages it.
transcripts.chapter: The first question asks what the club is called and what each of us has to do. Anne made the rules, so look at what she tells Marilla. The second wants Anne’s story in two sentences. Two! I heard every word of it, and I couldn’t. Keep the people and the ending. The third asks why a moral matters to her. Look at who she says agrees.
transcripts.workshop: Today you add. Find one place in your story where things happen too fast, where somebody falls or wins or cries and we never feel it. Then slow down and put in what we’d see or hear or feel. Anne’s stories are full of things happening, horses running away and people drowning. The part I love best is always the little bit in between. Put a little bit in.

a.raw: diana read annes story and cried during the saddest part
a.fixed: Diana read Anne’s story and cried during the saddest part.
a.why: A capital on the name Diana, an apostrophe-s on Anne’s because the story belongs to Anne, and a period at the end. Read is already in the past: same spelling, said like red.

b.raw: jane read rubys story and wept at the saddest part
b.fixed: Jane read Ruby’s story and wept at the saddest part.
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on Jane, an apostrophe-s on Ruby’s because the story is hers, and a period at the end. Wept is the past of weep, not weeped.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say which rule you think Anne cares about most, and why.
scholar.journal-q2: … then name one detail you left out on purpose, and why the summary works without it.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say whether Mr. and Mrs. Allan laughing “in the wrong places” means the moral worked.

fill1.h1: A truck takes goods across the country. Which root means to carry?
fill1.why: port means to carry: trans + port = to carry across.

fill2.h1: Selling to another country means sending goods out. Which root means to carry?
fill2.why: port means to carry: ex + port = to carry out.

fill3.h1: A magnet draws things toward it. Which root means to pull?
fill3.why: tract means to pull or draw: at + tract = to draw toward.

fill4.h1: When you lose focus, your attention gets pulled away. Which root means to pull?
fill4.why: tract means to pull or draw: dis + tract = to draw apart.

match.vanity: Vanity is about how a person looks and how much they care about it. Look for the meaning about too much pride in appearance.
match.implicitly: To believe someone implicitly is to believe them without asking a single question. Look for the meaning about trusting completely.
match.epoch: An epoch is a stretch of time people remember afterward. Look for the meaning about a turning point.
match.diligent: A diligent pupil keeps at her work and doesn’t skip the hard parts. Look for the meaning about working hard and carefully.

sort.sing → sang: Say them one after the other. Did the whole word change, or only the sound in the middle?
sort.drink → drank: The d, r, n and k all stayed put. Only one letter moved. Which column is that?
sort.begin → began: Begin and began share every letter but one. Which column is for one vowel moving?
sort.go → went: Go and went don’t share a single letter. That’s more than a vowel moving.
sort.am → was: Put am and was side by side. Is anything the same at all?
sort.put → put: Read both halves again. Did anything change?
sort.cut → cut: Today I cut, yesterday I cut. The same word both times. Which column is for that?
sort.cost → cost: Last year it cost a penny, and the word is just the same as the plain verb. Which column fits?
sort.courage → courageous: The suffix starts with o. Look closely: is the e still there?
sort.manage → manageable: The suffix starts with a. Has the e stayed, or gone?
sort.notice → noticing: The suffix starts with i. Look for the e. Is it still there?
sort.change → changing: The e has gone. Which letter does the suffix start with?
sort.hope → hoping: Is there a c or a g just before the e in hope? Look at what the third column is for.
sort.write → writing: Write ends in te, not ce or ge. There’s no soft sound to protect.

notes.wgrd: Summarizing means telling what happened without retelling everything. Keep the events that changed something, and leave out the small details.
vocab: Too much pride in how one looks; caring too much about appearance.
A memorable period of time; a turning point.
Working hard and carefully; not giving up.
notes.wordParts: port means “to carry” (transport, portable, export). tract means “to pull” or “to draw” (attract, distract, extract).
notes.grammar: Irregular past-tense verbs don’t just add -ed. Some change a vowel (sing → sang), some turn into a new word (go → went), and some don’t change at all (put → put).
notes.spelling: After ce or ge, keep the silent e when the suffix starts with a or o, so the c or g stays soft (courageous, manageable). Drop it when the suffix starts with e or i (noticing, changing).
